                    ### Question
                    A 12-year-old male presents to the pediatrician after two days of tea-colored urine which appeared to coincide with the first day of junior high football. He explains that he refused to go back to practice because he was humiliated by the other players due to his quick and excessive fatigue after a set of drills accompanined by pain in his muscles. A blood test revealed elevated creatine kinase and myoglobulin levels. A muscle biopsy was performed revealing large glycogen deposits and an enzyme histochemistry showed a lack of myophosphorylase activity. Which of the following reactions is not occuring in this individuals?

                    ### Options

opb. Breaking down glycogen to glucose-1-phosphate
opc. Cleaving alpha-1,6 glycosidic bonds from glycogen
opd. Creating alpha-1,6 glycosidic bonds in glycogen
ope. Converting galactose to galactose-1-phosphate

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient presents with symptoms consistent with McArdle's disease, characterized by myophosphorylase deficiency, leading to impaired glycogenolysis. This results in the accumulation of glycogen in muscle tissue, causing muscle fatigue and pain, as evidenced by elevated creatine kinase and myoglobulin levels. The key reactions affected by myophosphorylase deficiency include the inability to break down glycogen to glucose-1-phosphate and the inability to cleave alpha-1,4 glycosidic bonds. Therefore, the reaction that is not occurring in this individual is the conversion of glycogen to glucose-1-phosphate (option opb) and the cleaving of alpha-1,6 glycosidic bonds (option opc). The conversion of glucose-6-phosphate to glucose (option opa) and the creation of alpha-1,6 glycosidic bonds in glycogen (option opd) are not directly affected by myophosphorylase activity. The conversion of galactose to galactose-1-phosphate (option ope) is unrelated to glycogen metabolism and is not impacted by this condition. Thus, the most accurate answer is that the individual is not breaking down glycogen to glucose-1-phosphate.
